alignments.note: εἰ → if.
δέ → But.
ἡμῶν is present and free to take *our*, so rule 20 empties the article.
ἀδικία → unrighteousness.
ἡμῶν → our.
*of God* headed on the noun (rule 17).
Both Greek words are anarthrous, so under rule 58 the supplied determiner belongs to the noun.
συνίστησιν → commendeth.
τί → what.
Future with supplied subject and auxiliary, headed on the lexical verb (rules 9 and 17).
Interrogative μή, which the ASV marks by inversion alone; the *Is* is the copula the verbless clause would have required anyway and is not a supplied interrogative word (rules 44 and 64).

Verbless clause with a lexical-noun subject, so rule 63 gives the supplied copula to the predicate adjective; inversion is English word order and rule 53 refuses to read the copula off it. Discontinuous under rule 15.
No determiner for θεός (rule 23).
θεός → God.

Second attributive article whose head noun θεός is expressed and stands in front of it, so rule 31's test — τῷ θεῷ τῷ κτίσαντι → *God who created* — gives the supplied relativizer to the participle and leaves this article realizing nothing. Rule 90 blesses no unit in which a head noun is expressed, and rule 32's apposition clause reaches the same answer, θεός having already written the word the relative clause is predicated of. Reading ὁ ἐπιφέρων as substantival and giving it *who* under rule 90 is the competing analysis and is refused on both tests. A reference comparison will report this as a disagreement, which is not a correction.

ἐπιφέρων → *who visiteth with*: the supplied relativizer is the participle's helper under rules 7 and 31, the article standing in front of an expressed head noun. τὴν ὀργήν is the verb's accusative object, and rule 106's accusative arm keeps an English preposition standing over an accusative inside the verb's own unit, since an accusative has no case for it to realize; rule 21 says the same from the other side, a preposition licensed by something other than the governed word's own case not moving to that word merely because it stands in front of it. Headed on the verb word.
The ASV writes a bare *wrath* with no determiner, so the article realizes nothing (rule 23).
Bare *wrath*: the *with* belongs to ἐπιφέρων's own phrasal government under rule 106's accusative arm, not to this accusative object.

Complex prepositional frame *after the manner of* riding whole with the expressed Greek preposition (rule 67). Rule 67 leaves the head genuinely divided for a proper preposition; I take the prepositional word, and heading on *manner* remains defensible.
ἄνθρωπον → men.
Finite verb with supplied subject pronoun, headed on the lexical verb.

review_notes: Corrected: s015 ὁ was aligned to *who* under rule 90 as if substantival. It is a second attributive article governing the expressed θεός, so rule 31's main branch applies and the participle carries the relativizer. Both routes into the question — rule 31's expressed-head-noun test and rule 32's apposition clause — give the same answer, so the change is robust either way.

The earlier correction stands: *with* (t019) is inside ἐπιφέρων's unit, τὴν ὀργήν being an accusative object with no case for an English preposition to realize (rule 106's accusative arm, and rule 21 from the other side). ROM.3.11 reads ἐκζητῶν … τὸν θεόν → *seeketh after* / *God* the same way.
The κατὰ ἄνθρωπον frame is still headed on *after*; rule 67 records the corpus as genuinely divided on this head for a proper preposition, and *manner* remains defensible.
A reference comparison will now report s015 as a disagreement; rules 31 and 32 say that report is not a correction.
